title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
section: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Neural elds are a highly eective representation across visual computing. This work observes that tting these elds is greatly improved by incorporating spatial stochasticity during training, and that this simple technique can replace or even outperform custom-designed hierarchies and frequencyspace constructions. The approach is formalized as implicitly operating on a blurred version of the eld, evaluated in-expectation by sampling with Gaussian-distributed osets. Querying the blurred eld during optimization greatly improves convergence and robustness, akin to the role of preconditioners in numerical linear algebra. This implicit, sampling-based perspective ts naturally into the neural eld paradigm, comes at no additional cost, and is extremely simple to implement. We describe the basic theory of this technique, including details such as handling boundary conditions, and extending to a spatially-varying blur. Experiments demonstrate this approach on representations including coordinate MLPs, neural hashgrids, triplanes, and more, across tasks including surface reconstruction and radiance elds.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text:
Neural elds represent signals with a function mapping coordinates to signal values, promising an easy-to-optimize and spatiallyadaptive representation for signals such as signed distance functions, densities, and radiance elds in 3D, or even simply the color eld of an image in 2D. Many variants have been explored, but the most basic neural eld is a function parameterized as a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with weights which are t to encode the eld. Neural elds can allocate their capacity adaptively as-needed across the domain and benet from the repertoire of techniques common in machine learning, including auto-dierentiation, black-box optimizers, and ecient parallel evaluation on GPUs.
However, neural elds are not without challenges. Fitting a neural eld amounts to solving an expensive nonlinear optimization problem to train the neural network. This is true even when encoding an already-known signal, and is worsened when optimizing for indirect inverse problems, such as reconstruction from images. title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: The challenge of optimizing neural elds has led to a proliferation of variants in the representation, with alternate input encodings, architectures, hierarchies, and hybrid strategies, including the wellknown work of Mildenhall et al . [2021]; Müller et al . [2022]; Tancik et al . [2020], among many others. One perspective on these techniques is that they facilitate easier tting of the eld by improving the optimization landscape with a more suitable parameterization for the neural eld, or improvements in computational eciency and expressive power. However, improved representational power may even worsen the eects of local minima in the optimization process, especially in indirectly supervised and inverse problems with challenging objectives [Härenstam-Nielsen et al . 2024; Li et al . 2023; Yang et al . 2023]. More fundamentally, these many representational variants add signicant complexity, and are generally incompatible with one-another. The challenges of neural elds have also been addressed at the application level, with specialized coarse-to-ne optimization schemes, regularization terms and many other taskspecic optimization techniques [Härenstam-Nielsen et al .

In this paper, we propose a simple neural eld optimization technique that greatly alleviates the challenge of spurious local minima, improves quality, and can be easily integrated into a wide variety of representations and tasks. The basic idea is to stochastically perturb the input coordinates whenever querying the eld during optimization. From a principled perspective, this is equivalent in-expectation to sampling from a spatial blurring of the eld, yet this relationship is implicit and the approach has only the negligible computational cost of adding a small oset to each sample. We call this technique stochastic preconditioning (SP) in reference to the use of preconditioners in linear algebra, to emphasize its benets in improving the optimization landscape and its applicability to many problems.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Frequency domain. Neural eld representations quickly moved past naively encoding a eld in a MLP. One line of work leverages frequency-domain encodings of the input coordinates, enriching the input space with high-frequency features [Tancik et al . 2020]. The use of this technique for radiance elds [Mildenhall et al . 2021] was key to the broad adoption of neural elds, and continues to be eective in subsequent formulations [Wang et al . 2021]. SIREN [Sitzmann et al . 2020] builds an architecture entirely from periodic activations to exploit their properties, while BACON [Lindell et al . 2022], BANF [Shabanov et al . 2024] and TUNER [Hayes et al . 2023] deepen this perspective with explicit control over the frequency spectrum of the signal. Our stochastic preconditioning likewise leverages frequency-adapted optimization via a blur operation, but in a manner which is compatible with any neural eld architecture, and can be applied in conjunction with frequency-space representations for further improvements (Figure 2, Table 2).

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Another line of work considers signal processing-like operations on neural elds [Nsampi et al . 2023; Xu et al . 2022] including a related stochastic sampling perspective in [Rebain et al . 2024]; our work focuses on blurring as an optimization technique, rather than tasks where a ltered signal arises in the desired input or output.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Hybrid feature grids. Another approach is to augment the neural eld with trainable input features sampled from some backing store or grid [Fridovich-Keil and Yu et al . 2022]. Instant NGP [Müller et al . 2022] fetches features from a multi-resolution hashgrid encoding, a technique that has since become widely used for largescale and high-performance neural elds [Barron et al . 2023; Li et al . 2023; Takikawa et al . 2023a]. Though ecient, naively-applied hash-encoded neural elds seem particularly prone to spurious local minima—adding our stochastic preconditioning oers a signicant improvement (Figures 6). Triplane encodings map or learn 3D features to a triplet of planar grids orthogonal to the coordinate axes [Wang et al . 2023], while Karnewar et al . [2022] explore the limit case of a single nonlinearity applied directly to grid features without MLP. In both settings, our approach again has benets (Figure 2).

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Optimization. Rather than modifying the objective or architecture of any given problem, our approach modies the training process. Coarse-to-ne approaches have a long history in optimization, as well as specically in neural elds [Karnewar et al . 2022; Li et al . 2023; Mujkanovic et al . 2024; Xiangli et al . 2022; Yang et al . 2023], and several important downstream applications [Akgul and Kambhamettu 2003; Yao and Al-Dahle 2019]. Neural elds which leverage hierarchical feature stores [Takikawa et al . 2021] take particular advantage of coarse-to-ne optimization by adaptively unlocking levels of the hierarchy [Hertz et al . 2021; Karnewar et al . 2022; Li et al . 2023; Petit et al . 2025; Walker et al . 2024]. Yang et al . [2023] take a similar approach in the frequency-domain [Tancik et al . 2020], gradually increasing the frequency range of the input encoding. Seo et al . [2024] permute pixel coordinates on images to accelerate optimization.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Another work specically addresses the shortcomings of neural radiance eld training from a gradient scaling perspective [Philip and Deschaintre 2023]. These techniques are simple and eective, but specic to the internals of the representation— stochastic preconditioning oers similar coarse-to-ne optimization with a generic approach applicable to any neural eld.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Stochastic perturbations in machine learning. Perturbation of inputs during neural network training has a rich history in the machine learning literature. Sietsma and Dow [1991] rst proposed adding noise to network inputs to improve generalization, though in simpler settings. The theoretical foundations were later established by Bishop [1995], showing that input noise injection is equivalent to Tikhonov regularization for specic loss functions. Grandvalet et al . [1997] further connected Gaussian input noise to heat kernel diusion, providing additional theoretical guarantees. Adding noise to other quantities during training, such as the activations, was also explored [An 1996; Camuto et al . 2020]. While these classical works focus on perturbations to improve generalization and aim to provide theoretical guarantees in particular settings, our approach instead leverages stochastic smoothing specically to guide optimization trajectories and avoid local minima in the context of spatial neural elds.

text: Blurring the eld vs. blurring the supervision. An important subtlety of this approach is that we do not blur the supervision (groundtruth data), as has been explored in [Barron et al . 2021, 2023; Karnewar et al . 2022]. Rather, we blur the eld being optimized, as a preconditioner. The primary reason is that blurring the supervision is only possible in directly supervised problems such as tting to a known signal, whereas blurring the eld is fully general, and improves optimization even in regions where the eld is governed only by a regularizer (Section 5.1). Perhaps surprisingly, this more general approach still causes the eld 𝑓Ăto be optimized at low-frequencie rst (Figure 4). We hypothesize that this is because stochastic preconditioning damps high-frequency components, and thus also their gradients, during optimization.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text:
We validate and explore stochastic preconditioning on a range of neural eld representations and tasks. We make a distinction between indirectly supervised and directly supervised tasks. In an indirectly supervised task, the goal is to solve a nontrivial inverse problem guided by incomplete supervision; we consider surface reconstruction from images and oriented point clouds, and neural radiance elds (NeRFs). In directly supervised tasks, the goal is to encode an already-known signal into a neural eld; we consider signed distance functions and images. In general our method is most benecial in the indirectly supervised setting, as they are dicult optimization problems with many local minima.
In all experiments, we compare stochastic preconditioning to the baseline neural eld optimization at equal training iteration counts. Adding noise is computationally inexpensive, so there is otherwise little change to the runtime or other characteristics of a method, unless e.g., a hierarchy is intentionally removed, as in Section 5.2. For full details of experimental congurations and additional results, please see the supplemental text and included webpage .

A more challenging reconstruction task is to recover surfaces from posed images of a scene via dierentiable volumetric rendering of an SDF eld. Much work has adapted the NeRF-like [Mildenhall et al . 2021] formulation [Li et al . 2023; Oechsle et al . 2021; Wang et al . 2021; Yariv et al . 2021], dening volumetric density as a function of an SDF eld, and rendering that density along with auxiliary eld outputs for color or directional radiance. These approaches extract high-delity surfaces when successful, but can be challenging to t due to the dicult inverse nature of the problem.

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [Mildenhall et al . 2021] represent the appearance of a scene as a neural eld encoding the density and outgoing radiance from each point in space, rendered via volumetric sampling along rays. In Section 5.1.2 we already considered methods which optimize SDFs via NeRF-like rendering; the approaches here use more general density in place of SDFs, which may yield higher visual delity but lack an underlying surface representation.
We evaluate primarily on two cases where overtting artifacts are particularly likely to occur: sparse supervision and ReLU elds [Karnewar et al. 2022] without hierarchical training.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Sparse Supervision. First we consider the sparse-view scenario, tting NeRFs to a comparatively small number of images, which greatly exacerbates the optimization challenges of local minima and overtting to oater artifacts. We adopt the setting of FreeNeRF [Yang et al . 2023], a recent approach tackling this challenge via control of frequency-domain encoding and near-camera geometry. Figure 7 shows a comparison against ordinary MipNeRF [Barron et al . 2021] in this setting as a baseline, as as well as simply adding our stochastic preconditioning to MipNeRF. As expected, MipNeRF struggles in the sparse view scenario, but adding stochastic preconditioning yields high quality results on-par with FreeNeRF—and while FreeNerf is specic to frequency encodings, stochastic preconditioning is applicable to any underlying neural eld representation. See Table 5 in the supplement for additional metrics.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text:
ReLU Fields. ReLU elds [Karnewar et al . 2022] are a notably nonneural representation for NeRFs, exchanging the neural eld for a simple trilinearly-interpolated regular grid with a single ReLU nonlinearity after interpolation, akin to prior work optimizing directly on grids [Fridovich-Keil and Yu et al . 2022]. To successfully optimize NeRFs, ReLU elds leverage a coarse-to-ne approach, resulting in a four-stage pipeline where each stage uses a ner grid representation and higher-resolution target image; optimization fails catastrophically without this hierarchy. We nd that omitting the hierarchy and simply using stochastic preconditioning instead yields similar or better results (Figure 8).
In this particular experiment, we remove an existing the coarse-tone hierarchy and replace it with stochastic preconditioning—this simplies the approach, but comes at some cost of increased training time from 3.1 hours to 5.2 hours, since we no longer benet from fast iterations at the coarse level.

Here we analyze a few important aspects of our method: the initial alpha value, the choice of noise, and the number of stochastic samples used.
Choice of Initial Alpha. In Section 4.2 we suggest a default policy of scheduling the preconditioning blur scale Ă from Ă0 = 2% of the domain bounding box diagonal down to Ă = 0 during the rst 1/3 of train-

This policy was found experimentally: the inset gure shows a study in the setting of Section 5.1, each light line corresponds to a dierent input object, the horizontal axis varies the Ă0 schedule value, and the vertical axis plots the resulting quality (lower is better). title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Choice of Noise. We default to using Gaussian noise when applying stochastic preconditioning in our experiments for its formal relationship to blur operators, the spectral domain, and heat ow. We additionally experiment with other noise kernels such as uniform and squared Gaussian noise, for surface reconstruction from points as in Section 5.1 and nd largely similar results for all kernels, yielding mean Chamfer distance error of 9.1e-4 with a Gaussian kernel, 9.3e-4 with a uniform kernel, and 8.8e-4 with a squared-Gaussian kernel. See the complete set of metrics in Table 7 in Supplement.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text: Single Sample v.s. Multiple Samples. Our method proposes stochastic preconditioning in expectation, via a single perturbed sample. However, we also experiment taking additional samples, to moreaccurately estimate approximate the blurred eld at each evaluation. In computation, this amounts to averaging multiple samples from Ĝ (Į + Ă) with independent Ă ∽ N (0, Ă). Taking additional samples linearly increases cost, but we do not observe any benet, likely due to the stochasticity already inherent in neural eld optimization. In the ReLU eld setting as in Section 5.2, we observe an average PSNR of 33.72 with single sample, 33.74 with two samples, and 33.79 with four samples. See Table 6 in the Supplement for full results.

text: Small changes to hyperparameters can easily make the dierence between success and getting trapped in a poor local minimum, especially for indirectly supervised tasks. To explore this eect, we take the NeuS with hashgrid conguration on one scene from Section 5.1.2, and sweep through several choices of network learning rate, hashgrid learning rate, maximum resolution of the hashgrid, and hash table size. For each parameter conguration, we t the eld with and without stochastic preconditioning, and measure the nal PSNR. Figure 9 shows a clear distribution shift—although even stochastic preconditioning does not succeed for all choices of hyperparameters, it succeeds much more often across a wider range of hyperparameters. This also provides evidence that the improvement oered by stochastic preconditioning is not an artifact of one particular choice of hyperparameters.

title: Stochastic Preconditioning for Neural Field Optimization
text:
Limitations and future work. Stochastic sampling is an unbiased estimator for the blurred eld, but sampling a nonlinear loss function with a single sample is a biased estimator for the loss on the true blurred eld. We do not observe this to cause problems in practice, but there is opportunity for deeper analysis. Although stochastic preconditioning improves quality at no additional cost, it misses out on some accelerations oered by hierarchical schemes—optimizing a low-resolution level of a hierarchy is typically very cheap, but applying stochastic preconditioning with a large blur has the same cost as optimizing the full eld. We only briey investigate spatiallyvarying noise distributions (Section 5.5); future work may explore additional strategies, including anisotropic distributions, as well as other uses for the optimized Ă maps
Conclusion. We believe that stochastic preconditioning will serve as a valuable tool in the neural elds toolbox, easily deployed to improve performance on a wide variety of problems at minimal cost, especially when custom-designed approaches may be cumbersome.

We believe this calls for a reexamination of this widely-used objective function, for example incorporating an Eikonal constraint. This is, however, outside the scope of this paper.

https://github.com/akanimax/thr3ed_atom The rst baseline is the unmodied ReLU eld method, which contains a four-stage hierarchical training schedule for coarse-tone optimization. In the second baseline, we remove this hierarchical training schedule.
Hyperparameters. We follow the hyperparameters used in the original ReLU eld experiment. Specically, we use a dense grid of resolution 256 × 256 × 256 and optimize with the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0 . 03. The original ReLU eld baseline employs a hierarchical training curriculum in which the grid is initially optimized at a resolution reduced by a factor of 2 4 . The grid is trained for 7,000 iterations per-stage, then is upsampled by a factor of two after each stage. The grid features is trilinearly-interpolated to initialize the grid for next stage. Note that the learning rate exponentially decreases per stage after 3,000 steps.

We use it for importance sampling during training. In addition, we use it for adaptive hashgrid feature masking such that the number of levels of the hashgrid feature used at a query position is inversely related to the magnitude of the optimized Ă value.
